```{r setup, include = FALSE}
if (requireNamespace("albersdown", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ggplot2::theme_set(albersdown::theme_albers(params$family))
}
# Package vignettes embed their figures, so CRAN copies use a lower
# resolution to keep the package small; the pkgdown site keeps the default.
if (!identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dpi = 72)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
library(eyesim)
library(ggplot2)
```

In a memory reinstatement study, people first study a set of images and later
see them again. A natural question is whether a test fixation lands where *this
person* looked when studying *this image*, beyond where they look in general.
This vignette answers that question at the level of single fixations:

1. Build study density maps, one per person and item.
2. Combine them into four **leave-out reference maps** for each person/item.
3. Pair every test fixation (the *case*) with **control** locations.
4. Score cases and controls against each reference and compare them.
5. Repeat the comparison with a **mismatched** study map as a baseline.

Steps 3 and 5 involve random draws. The package returns them as explicit
tables, so an analysis can be saved, replayed, or rescored under a different
choice without new randomness.

## The example data

We simulate eight people (`s1`–`s8`) studying six items (`i1`–`i6`). Each
person/item pair has its own preferred location, drawn at random. Study
fixations cluster tightly around it, and the six test fixations for that pair
return to it more loosely. Nothing else links people or items, so only a
person's own study map of an item should predict where they look at test.

<details>
<summary>Show the simulation code</summary>

```{r synthetic-data}
set.seed(53)
study <- expand.grid(subject = paste0("s", 1:8), item = paste0("i", 1:6),
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
centers <- cbind(runif(nrow(study), 20, 80), runif(nrow(study), 20, 80))

# One fixation_group of 12 study fixations per person/item pair.
study$fixgroup <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(study)), function(i) {
  fixation_group(
    x = rnorm(12, centers[i, 1], 5), y = rnorm(12, centers[i, 2], 5),
    onset = seq(0, 1100, 100), duration = rep(100, 12)
  )
})

# Six test fixations per pair, one trial per item.
test <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(study)), function(i) {
  data.frame(subject = study$subject[i], item = study$item[i],
             trial = study$item[i], epoch = "test",
             x = rnorm(6, centers[i, 1], 7),
             y = rnorm(6, centers[i, 2], 7), onset = seq(0, 500, 100))
}))
```

</details>

The study data hold one `fixation_group` per person/item pair. The test data
are an ordinary table with one row per fixation:

```{r show-test}
head(test, 3)
```

```{r plot-fixations, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 5.8, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "Study fixations (dots) and test fixations (crosses) for two people and three items. Each person returns to their own study location; the two people prefer different locations for the same item."}
show_subjects <- c("s1", "s2")
show_items <- c("i1", "i2", "i3")
shown <- study$subject %in% show_subjects & study$item %in% show_items
study_fix <- do.call(rbind, lapply(which(shown), function(i) {
  data.frame(subject = study$subject[i], item = study$item[i],
             x = study$fixgroup[[i]]$x, y = study$fixgroup[[i]]$y)
}))
test_fix <- subset(test, subject %in% show_subjects & item %in% show_items)

fix_both <- rbind(cbind(study_fix, phase = "Study"),
                  cbind(test_fix[c("subject", "item", "x", "y")], phase = "Test"))

ggplot(fix_both, aes(x, y, colour = phase, shape = phase)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = phase), stroke = 1) +
  facet_grid(subject ~ item, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Study = "#2166ac", Test = "#b2182b"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Study = 16, Test = 4), name = NULL) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(Study = 1.2, Test = 2), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 50, 100)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 50, 100)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y")
```

## Study density maps

`density_by()` smooths each person's study fixations for each item into a
density map on a shared 20 × 20 grid. With bounds of 2.5 and 97.5, the grid
points are the centres of 5-unit cells tiling the 0–100 range. Here only fixation time between 50 and 950 ms counts,
and a fixation that straddles a window edge contributes just its overlapping
duration.

```{r study-maps}
maps <- density_by(
  study, groups = c("subject", "item"), sigma = 8,
  xbounds = c(2.5, 97.5), ybounds = c(2.5, 97.5), outdim = c(20, 20),
  window = c(50, 950), window_weight = "overlap", duration_weighted = TRUE
)
```

```{r plot-maps, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.4, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "Study density maps for the same panels, with the test fixations overlaid. Test fixations fall on the bright region of the matching map."}
map_frame <- function(map, ...) {
  data.frame(expand.grid(x = map$x, y = map$y), z = as.vector(map$z), ...)
}
shown_maps <- which(maps$subject %in% show_subjects & maps$item %in% show_items)
map_cells <- do.call(rbind, lapply(shown_maps, function(i) {
  map_frame(maps$density[[i]], subject = maps$subject[i], item = maps$item[i])
}))

ggplot(map_cells, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = z)) +
  geom_point(data = test_fix, colour = "white", shape = 4, size = 2, stroke = 1) +
  facet_grid(subject ~ item, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Density", option = "magma") +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_eyesim_spatial()
```

A fixation is scored by looking up the grid point nearest to it. There is no
interpolation between grid points; locations beyond the grid take the edge value.

## Leave-out reference maps

A person's own study map is the obvious predictor of their test fixations. On its
own, though, it cannot separate memory for this specific image from two other
sources. One is a habit of looking at the same places in every image. The other
is image content that draws everyone's gaze. `reference_maps()` therefore builds
four maps for each person/item pair. Each one leaves out a different part of the
data:

| Reference | Built from | High where... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `self_item` | this person's study map of this item | this person looked at this image |
| `self_other_items` | this person's maps of the *other* items | this person tends to look in any image |
| `others_item` | *other people's* maps of this item | this image draws everyone's gaze |
| `others_other_items` | other people's maps of other items | people look in general (e.g. a centre bias) |

```{r references}
refs <- reference_maps(maps, floor = 1 / (10 * 20 * 20))
refs
```

```{r plot-references, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.6, fig.cap = "The four references for person s1 and item i1, with s1's test fixations on i1 overlaid. Only the own-item reference concentrates where those fixations land."}
target <- which(refs$keys$subject == "s1" & refs$keys$item == "i1")
ref_cells <- do.call(rbind, lapply(refs$refs, function(r) {
  map_frame(reference_map(refs, row = target, ref = r), reference = r)
}))
ref_cells$reference <- factor(ref_cells$reference, levels = refs$refs)
target_fix <- subset(test, subject == "s1" & item == "i1")

ggplot(ref_cells, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = z)) +
  geom_point(data = target_fix, colour = "white", shape = 4, size = 1.8, stroke = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~reference, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "log score", option = "magma") +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_eyesim_spatial()
```

The other three references are broad or multi-lobed here. Each averages
several study maps whose preferred locations are unrelated, because this
simulation gives people and items nothing in common. Their mass sits centrally
only because every simulated location lies between 20 and 80. In real data
these references carry viewing habits, image content and centre bias.
Comparing a fixation's scores across all four is informative, but the scores
are correlated. Separating their contributions requires a statistical model
chosen by the researcher; the package does not decompose them automatically.

**How the maps are combined.** By default each study map is scaled to sum to 1,
transformed to `log(density + floor)`, and only then averaged across
contributors. The `floor` is a required small offset that keeps empty cells
finite. For unit-sum maps, `1 / (10 * ncells)` is a reasonable starting point,
but it changes the scores, so the package never chooses it silently. For
`others_other_items`, each other person's items are averaged first and those
person means are then averaged with equal weight. A person with more items
therefore does not count more. Use `space = "density"` to average densities
instead of log values, and add `transform = "log"` to take the log after
averaging.

**Missing data.** A `NULL` map counts as missing, not as an empty map.
`refs$counts` records how many maps (self references) or people (other
references) contributed to each reference. Any reference with fewer than
`min_n` contributors yields `NA` scores, and its row is kept. `reference_map()`
returns any single map for inspection, as in the figure above.

## Controls: where else could the person have looked?

A high score for a test fixation means little unless locations the person did
*not* fixate score lower. `sample_controls()` pairs each test fixation (the
*case*) with control locations. By default the controls are the same person's
fixations from other trials, so they share that person's general viewing habits.

```{r controls}
strata <- sample_controls(test, n = 10, draws = 3, stratify_by = "epoch", seed = 7)
print(head(strata[c("subject", "item", "case_id", "control_id", "draw",
                    "is_case", "x", "y")], 4), row.names = FALSE)
```

Each case forms a *stratum* with its 10 controls. This is repeated for three
independent control draws. `x` and `y` are each row's own location, and
`control_id` is the row of `test` it was taken from (its *donor*; a case row
points to itself). The remaining columns describe the case. Controls come from the same
subject and epoch. They exclude the case's own trial and every trial showing the
same item, so repeated presentations of an item cannot donate controls that sit
on its own hotspots.

```{r plot-controls, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 4.4, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "One test fixation (cross) and its ten controls from the first draw (circles), over the case's own-item reference. The controls are s1's fixations on other items."}
one_case <- subset(strata, case_id == strata$case_id[1] & draw == 1)
own_cells <- subset(ref_cells, reference == "self_item")

ggplot(own_cells, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = z)) +
  geom_point(data = subset(one_case, !is_case), shape = 21, colour = "white",
             fill = "#2166ac", size = 2.4, stroke = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = subset(one_case, is_case), colour = "white", shape = 4,
             size = 3.5, stroke = 1.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "log score", option = "magma") +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_eyesim_spatial()
```

Other designs call for other comparison locations. `method = "uniform"` draws
controls uniformly within explicit bounds. `method = "map"` draws grid locations
from a supplied density, always with replacement. These choices answer different
questions. There is deliberately no option to jitter controls away from cases:
moving only the controls can create an apparent preference where none exists.

## Scores and case–control contrasts

`score_strata()` looks up every case and control location in all four
references. `case_control_contrast()` then subtracts the mean control score from
the case score in each stratum and averages these differences within each trial:

```{r scoring}
scored <- score_strata(strata, refs)
contrasts <- case_control_contrast(scored, by = "trial")
head(contrasts, 3)
```

A positive contrast means the person's test fixations score higher than their
controls under that reference. Before the comparison, scores are standardized
within each subject and control draw (see
[Reusing the scaling](#reusing-the-scaling)), so contrasts are in z units.

```{r plot-contrasts, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Trial contrasts for each reference (one point per person, item and control draw), with their means. Only the own-item reference separates test fixations from controls in the expected direction."}
contrast_long <- data.frame(
  reference = factor(rep(refs$refs, each = nrow(contrasts)), levels = rev(refs$refs)),
  contrast = unlist(contrasts[refs$refs], use.names = FALSE)
)
contrast_means <- aggregate(contrast ~ reference, contrast_long, mean)

ggplot(contrast_long, aes(contrast, reference)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, width = 0, alpha = 0.35, size = 1, colour = "#2166ac") +
  geom_point(data = contrast_means, shape = 124, size = 7, colour = "#b2182b") +
  labs(x = "Case minus control score (z units)", y = NULL)
```

```{r check-contrasts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(contrast_means$contrast[contrast_means$reference == "self_item"] > 1,
          abs(contrast_means$contrast[contrast_means$reference == "others_item"]) < 0.3,
          abs(contrast_means$contrast[contrast_means$reference == "others_other_items"]) < 0.3)
```

The own-item contrast is large and positive, as planted. The two "other people"
contrasts are near zero. `self_other_items` is *negative* even though this
simulation contains no viewing habit. The controls are this person's test
fixations on the other items, and they land on the hotspots of that person's
study maps of those items, which are exactly the maps averaged into
`self_other_items`. The controls therefore score higher than the case. With
same-person observed controls, this reference cannot reveal a viewing habit,
because the controls share it by construction. `method = "uniform"` controls
are needed if that is the question.

Control draws are kept separate in the output. Averaging over them is an
explicit analysis choice:

```{r draw-means}
aggregate(contrasts[refs$refs], list(control_draw = contrasts$draw), mean)
```

## A mismatched-item baseline

Even in the absence of item-specific memory, a person's own study map of a
*different* item can predict some test fixations, through habits or shared
image structure. A useful baseline therefore rescores each test trial against
a mismatched study map from the same person. `mismatch_assignments()` draws the
replacement items, and `mismatch_draws()` rescores with them:

```{r mismatch}
assignments <- mismatch_assignments(strata, refs, n = 20, seed = 31)
print(head(assignments, 3), row.names = FALSE)

null <- mismatch_draws(strata, refs, assignments = assignments,
                       replace_ref = "self_item", by = "trial")
```

Each of the 20 null draws assigns every trial one replacement item, used for all
of that trial's fixations and control draws. With
`replace_ref = "self_item"`, only the own-item reference is swapped;
`replace_ref = "all"` swaps the whole set of four references.

Mismatching changes which controls are fair. A control taken from the
replacement item's trial would sit on the replacement map's hotspots and push
the mismatched contrast below zero. `mismatch_draws()` therefore drops, in each
draw, the controls taken from either the case's item or the replacement item.
`null$contrasts` holds the mismatched contrasts. `null$paired_observed` rescores
the *matched* map using exactly the same retained controls and scaling, so the
two can be compared directly:

```{r plot-mismatch, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 5.6, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Mean own-item contrast in each of the 20 null draws, for the matched study map and for a mismatched one, scored against the same retained controls. Lines join the two results from the same draw."}
draw_means <- function(x, label) {
  out <- aggregate(self_item ~ null_draw, x, mean)
  out$template <- label
  out
}
paired <- rbind(draw_means(null$paired_observed, "Matched item"),
                draw_means(null$contrasts, "Mismatched item"))
paired$template <- factor(paired$template, levels = c("Matched item", "Mismatched item"))

ggplot(paired, aes(template, self_item)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(aes(group = null_draw), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = template), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2166ac", "#b2182b"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean own-item contrast (z units)")
```

```{r check-mismatch, include = FALSE}
matched <- mean(null$paired_observed$self_item)
mismatched <- mean(null$contrasts$self_item)
stopifnot(is.finite(matched), is.finite(mismatched), matched > mismatched + 1,
          matched > mean(contrasts$self_item),
          abs(mismatched) < 0.3)
```

The mismatched contrasts sit near zero, while the matched contrasts on the same
controls remain well above it. That gap is the planted item-specific
preference. The matched values (mean `r round(matched, 2)`) are higher than the own-item
mean in the previous section (`r round(mean(contrasts$self_item), 2)`). Each draw scores fewer controls and rescales
with the fit to its mismatched scores, so the two numbers are not directly
comparable. `null$observed` keeps the original contrasts on all controls. If
the strata were drawn with `item = NULL` and items repeat, those original
contrasts can still be attenuated by own-item controls.

`mismatch_draws()` returns these draws and their assignments, not p-values.
Whether swapping items gives a valid null depends on the design: repeated
items and condition differences can violate exchangeability. An own-item
contrast can also contain image-content effects, so compare it with the other
references before reading it as person-specific reinstatement.

## Reusing the scaling {#reusing-the-scaling}

`score_strata()` standardizes each reference within subject and control draw,
using all case and control scores. This is not the same as z-scoring the cells
of a map. The fitting step is also available separately, so the same scaling
can be saved and applied again:

```{r fitted-scaling}
raw <- score_strata(strata, refs, standardize = "none")
scaling <- fit_score_scaling(raw, by = c("subject", "draw"))
replayed <- apply_score_scaling(raw, scaling)
identical(replayed, scored)
```

Each control draw has its own fit, so adding draws later does not change the
scaling of earlier ones. A reference whose scores are constant within a group
maps to zero, missing scores stay missing (and make the contrast missing), and
applying a fit to a group it has not seen is an error.

## Details and options

**Saving and replaying.** Seeded functions restore the caller's random-number
state, and scoring uses no randomness. Saving `strata`, `assignments` and
`refs` (for example with `saveRDS()`) is enough to reproduce every number
above. The donor metadata (the `control_sources` attribute) survives
`saveRDS()` and subsetting with `[`, so a saved subset of cases can still be
traced to its controls. `subset()` and export to CSV drop it.

**Item exclusion.** `sample_controls()` detects an `item` column
automatically. Pass `item = "stimulus"` for another column name, or
`item = NULL` to exclude only the case's own trial. With the default
`replace = "auto"`, controls are drawn with replacement only when too few are
available, and an empty pool is an error.

**Mismatch controls.** `mismatch_draws()` drops controls without redrawing
them, so a stratum can run out, which is an error. The exclusion also applies
to strata drawn with `item = NULL`, so own-item controls are always dropped and
such strata can run out too. A subject who saw only two test
items cannot support a comparison between those two items with observed
controls, however many trials or controls there are. With
`control_policy = "fixed"`, every supplied control is kept, including those
from the replacement item. Combined with `sample_controls(..., item = NULL)`,
this gives an item-discrimination baseline. Under a real effect that baseline
is negative, so it should not be read as the level expected without
reinstatement.

**Scaling in the null.** By default each null draw refits the scaling on its
retained mismatched scores and applies it to both members of the pair.
`restandardize = FALSE` applies the original fit to both instead, and
`standardize = "none"` keeps raw reference units.

**Related functions.** `sample_density()` samples a single density map, and
also accepts a named list or table of maps.
`template_sample()` and `sample_density_time()` share the same map preparation
and lookup. Use the strata and assignment tables above when the identities of
controls and replacement draws need to be kept.
